---
title: "'We're just kind of stuck with them': IDOC inmates add pressure to already-crowded jail"
source: "https://www.idahopress.com/news/were-just-kind-of-stuck-with-them-idoc-inmates-add-pressure-to-already-crowded-jail/article_254cbc38-2438-4099-9bb3-10bb60374e71.html?emci=8543b2c3-5e43-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&emdi=9b698844-c243-f111-8ef2-000d3a14b640&ceid=110103"
author:
  - "[[MATTHEW NEIL WELLS mwells@idahopress.com]]"
published: 2026-04-27
created: 2026-07-08
description: "Canyon County Sheriff's Office shows how jail becoming more difficult to operate amid rising inmate population, including those being held for the state prison system."
---
CALDWELL — The Canyon County Jail houses inmates of varying degree, from inmates charged with low-level felonies to the most violent of crime. In addition to offenders who come from inside the county, it also hosts Idaho Department of Correction (IDOC) inmates.

Overcrowding is a serious concern. According to Canyon County statistics, the jail is 87.4% full, with 457 of 523 inmates locked inside. But the statistics also say the jail’s “optimal operation capacity” is 80%.

Joe Decker, public information officer for Canyon County Sheriff’s Office, tells the Idaho Press that the “optimal capacity for jails is 80% to allow for proper inmate classification, separation and safety.”

**UNIT A**

While there are bigger spaces than Pod One’s Unit A, Dale G. Haile Detention Center houses its worst offenders there.

“Everybody (in Unit A) is charged with murder and rape, or something along those lines,” said Capt. Harold Patchett of the Canyon County Sheriff’s Office. “We can’t house them with anybody else. They’re in single cells.”

The rules are the most strict for those individuals. Patchett said they’re out of their cells for one hour, by themselves, in a “day room.” They also spend one hour outside by themselves. That’s if it’s not raining.

In addition to Unit A, there are other units within the pod. Those are for high-medium security.

“They’re locked down most of the day based off of their charges,” Patchett said. “And these guys come out two or three at a time versus just one at a time.”

The deputy station within the pod has little room for deputies. The darkened windows let the deputies see the inmates and monitor for any potential fights, but the windows don’t provide clear sight for the inmates to look at the deputies.

The deputies also face a challenge: The toilet, steps below the station itself, includes only a curtain for privacy.

“That’s one of the huge challenges in here, is that’s the bathroom,” Patchett said. “If you have a male and female working in here, not many people want to use the bathroom in front of other people.”

Then there is the pod’s discipline area, which houses a limited number of cells.

“If we do have a male inmate written up for fighting, or something along those lines, they would go into a lockdown unit,” Patchett said.

Patchett said if there is a disciplinary issue, the jail has a team that conducts an interview with the inmate. They watch the video of the incident, then they watch the deputy’s body camera footage, and then they determine whether the inmate’s guilty or not.

“So it’s a good process,” Patchett said.

The inmates there are handcuffed before showering, making phone calls to family and filing grievances.

Patchett said it’s “super challenging with sex offenders right now.”

“The sex offender population is on the rise,” Patchett said. “And so we’re really struggling with trying to find room for that classification. We’ve kind of converted a couple living units to fit that need.”

Patchett said having that type of offender “causes problems” within the jail. There’s still a hierarchy of sorts with inmates. The sex offenders are the lowest class in jail.

**FEMALE UNITS**

Patchett showed a female unit before explaining how the jail tried temporary trailers but that they had “maintenance issues” with those.

![Canyon County Jail officials detail deficiencies](https://bloximages.chicago2.vip.townnews.com/idahopress.com/content/tncms/assets/v3/editorial/a/3c/a3c68e78-50a7-40b6-94fa-2321305c277a/69ebf380aa259.image.jpg)

Canyon County Jail officials detail deficiencies

### Canyon County Jail officials detail deficiencies

“We had to do some adjustments and move females back in this area,” Patchett said. “We have three open dormitories, and then one that’s locked down for disciplinary, and stuff like that.”

Patchett said there are about 80 women inside the jail, compared to about 400 men.

“But it can change daily,” Patchett said.

**WORKING WITH IDAHO DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTION**

Hosting IDOC inmates, in addition to the county inmates, isn’t something Patchett likes having to worry about.

“We house a lot of IDOC inmates, but we don’t want to,” Patchett said. “We ask (the state) to move the (IDOC inmates) out as soon as they can, but we’re averaging about 100 at any time who are ready to go at any time.”

Patchett said the county doesn’t contract with the state to house anybody.

“We’re just kind of stuck with them,” Patchett said.

The removal from the jail to an IDOC prison depends on when IDOC “has the bed space to take them,” Patchett said.

It can be “six months to a year, at least,” before those inmates get placed in a prison, according to Patchett.

**CHALLENGES FACING DEPUTIES**

Canyon County Sheriff’s Office Lt. Russ Donnelly spoke a little about the hardest thing deputies face day-in and day-out when working the jail.

“I think it would just be the amount of inmates to manage per deputy,” Donnelly said. “And then it depends on the housing unit.”

So if there’s a pod distant from another pod — where an incident has taken place — they need to rush over there. Some pods have regular rotations, such as Pod One. But that pod has fewer inmates, and more rotations. But another pod could have more inmates and fewer rotations.

Donnelly said “as a general rule,” on a normal day, “it’s not that bad.”

While there are security cameras, deputies still have to watch and operate them.

Pod Five is “a tent-like structure” that houses the inmates charged with the lowest-level felony offenses, like felony drug charges.

“We don’t typically hold anybody on a misdemeanor,” Patchett said. “Those ones are all cited and released.”

It’s a general population unit and is “considered a direct supervision unit,” according to Patchett. The pod holds 122 inmates in an “open dormitory” fashion. Even though the lowest-level offenders live there, they may be awaiting a court date and possibly release, the pod still has its own problems.

“If somebody is going to Pod Five, we have to walk them across the street,” Patchett said. “If somebody in Pod Five is going to court, we have to walk them (back) across the street. So it’s a little problematic (because of) people who try to escape.”

Patchett said the jail staff has seen several inmates try to escape while in handcuffs, but staff catches them “fairly quickly.”

And then there is the issue of smuggling, which the [Idaho Press reported on in early December](https://www.idahopress.com/news/canyon-county-jail-staff-stops-inmates-from-smuggling-meth-into-the-center/article_432f40f9-2cc2-4b0b-8c58-dea16f377336.html). Patchett gave an example of how problematic it has been in the past. It sounds as though the jail staff found a fix.

“Basically anyone can act like a bookstore, and so they ship the books in, and the books will be covered with, the pages will be laced with, drugs,” Patchett said. “And so we did away with all paper books. They’re all now on tablets.”

Patchett said another challenge is trying to convince people to work a jail.

At least for Canyon County Sheriff’s Office, the entry-level deputies start in the detention center, Donnelly said.

“I think there’s a benefit to starting in the jail,” Donnelly said. “It’s 72 and sunny every day, right?”

**Matthew Neil Wells** is the Nampa reporter at the Idaho Press. He covers city government, crime, features, profiles on people, and events. You can follow him on X @MatthewNWells, and email him at [mwells@idahopress.com](mailto:mwells@idahopress.com).
